messages.content:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: 240 {A1} of 240 {A2} shopper totals do not reconcile with the purchases behind them. The widest is short by 1,297.31 {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase was recorded at 2026-10-19T08:54:00Z {A4}. Found by the spend-integrity check, which runs every 7 {A5} days, so the fault is up to that old.
Alert raised: 2026-10-26T08:52:13Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged.
The alert rule fires as soon as its condition holds. The alert came 6 days 23 hours 58 minutes 13 seconds {alerted_after_the_onset} after the onset.
Broken from 2026-10-19T08:54:00Z {began} (the onset). The service was not back to normal by 2026-10-26T08:52:46Z {argus_stopped}, so it was broken for at least 6 days 23 hours 58 minutes 46 seconds {duration} - a lower bound, not a measurement, and every impact figure below is bounded the same way.
Argus held the incident for 33 seconds {held}, until 2026-10-26T08:52:46Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
Error rate: not measured by the metrics - metrics were read, but none from the hour before the onset, so there is no calm level to measure a rise against.
Customer loss: none so far - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all; a lower bound, counted with the service not seen back to normal.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-10-26T08:52:13Z {T1.1} Argus: Received SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-10-26T08:52:14Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-10-26T08:52:14Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-10-26T08:52:15Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 08:52:13 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-10-26T08:52:17Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 360 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-10-26T08:52:17Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at Oct 19 08:54 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-10-26T08:52:17Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB, started at Oct 25 20:52:12 {T7.3}, after the onset
  - [T8] 2026-10-26T08:52:34Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 8 {T8.2} days 8 {T8.3} hours 52 {T8.4} minutes 13 {T8.5} seconds before Oct 26 08:52:13 {T8.6}
  - [T9] 2026-10-26T08:52:34Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 1 {T9.2} production change
  - [T10] 2026-10-26T08:52:40Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's log lines, the 15 {T10.2} minutes before Oct 19 09:05 {T10.3}
  - [T11] 2026-10-26T08:52:40Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 0 {T11.2} log lines
  - [T12] 2026-10-26T08:52:46Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 2 {T12.2} candidate causes, best first: C1, C2
  - [T13] 2026-10-26T08:52:46Z {T13.1} Investigator Agent: Read every channel available
  - [T14] 2026-10-26T08:52:46Z {T14.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 1 {T14.2} flag change by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T14.3} hour before Oct 19 08:54 {T14.4}
  - [T15] 2026-10-26T08:52:46Z {T15.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on the leading candidate
  - [T16] 2026-10-26T08:52:46Z {T16.1} Argus: Refused to act - nothing would say whether the action that would test the candidate worked inside the time Argus waits, so it is recommended rather than taken
  - [T17] 2026-10-26T08:52:46Z {T17.1} Argus: Left for a person to do - putting monthly-spend-feature back
  - [T18] 2026-10-26T08:52:46Z {T18.1} Argus: Moved the incident to RECOMMENDED - action recommended
  - [T19] 2026-10-26T08:55:31Z {T19.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/355

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-10-19T08:52:00Z {P1.1} flag-toggle monthly-spend-feature by admin: feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on
  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - Read; none came back.

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - cite them; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1, also C2] Candidates blaming the same move of monthly-spend-feature, each reading it as a different kind of failure - different accounts of what it did, not one cause counted twice - each in its own words:
      C1: The monthly-spend-feature flag was switched on at 2026-10-19T08:52:00Z {C1.1}. Shopper spend totals written from then on disagree with the purchases behind them, and 240 {C1.2} of 240 {C1.3} totals are now wrong. The service itself serves normally, and the stored totals are what is wrong. [silent-data-corruption, confidence 0.6 {C1.4}, never tried: nothing would say whether the action that would test the candidate worked inside the time Argus waits, so it is recommended rather than taken]
      C2: Switching monthly-spend-feature on at 2026-10-19T08:52:00Z {C1.5} changed how spend totals are computed, and the totals have been wrong since the first purchase after it. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.3 {C1.6}, never tried: nothing would say whether the action that would test the candidate worked inside the time Argus waits, so it is recommended rather than taken]

Actions it took:
  - none

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault is in src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py. When `record_a_purchase` gets `derive_the_month=True`, it calls `record_purchase_deriving_the_month`. That function adds the purchase to the history and moves `total_cents`, but on purpose it never writes `total_this_month_cents` (its docstring says "without the month's total being moved"). So every purchase written through that path left the stored month total short by that purchase's price. The flag-off path, `record_purchase`, does add the price. That fits the investigation's evidence: after monthly-spend-feature was switched on, 240 {F1.1} of 240 {F1.2} totals no longer reconciled with their purchases, while errors and latency stayed flat.
      
      The fix: in src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py, `record_purchase_deriving_the_month` now sets `total_this_month_cents` to the sum of `price_cents` over the purchases in the updated history whose `in_current_month` is true. The path still keeps no running month figure that a write could forget to add to. Because the figure is derived from the history, an account whose stored total is already short is corrected by its next write on this path. `record_purchase` is unchanged, `record_a_purchase` keeps its signature, and nothing in this module reads a flag. So the code is safe with the flag on and with it off.
      
      The test: tests/io_shop/test_purchase_ledger.py gains cases that call `record_a_purchase(..., derive_the_month=True)`. They check four things: the month total includes a new in-month purchase, a purchase from an earlier month leaves the month total alone, a total that is already short is brought back to the sum of its in-month purchases, and after a run of writes `reconcile_monthly_totals` reports no disagreement. Against the code as it stood, the first case would get 0 {F1.3} where it expects 500 {F1.4}. Nobody has run these tests.
      
      The repair: scripts/repair_monthly_spend_totals.py is a one-off script. **It has not been run, and a person has to run it.** It reads accounts as JSON lines in the shape of `io_shop.accounts.Account`. That export format is an assumption, because I found no storage layer in what I read. The script picks out disagreeing accounts with `reconcile_monthly_totals` and sets each one's `total_this_month_cents` to the sum of its in-month purchases. By default it only reports what it would change. It writes the corrected accounts only when given `--write OUTPUT`, never changes its input, and leaves loading the output back into the store to whoever runs it. Deploy this patch and run the repair before switching the flag back on.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus:
  - [U1] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py:650, in the_mean_purchase_this_month: divides with it: account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought)
  - [U2] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py:882, in _compared_with_usual: reads it: this_month_cents = account.total_this_month_cents
  - [U3] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py:918, in render_monthly_statement: reads it: month_total_cents = account.total_this_month_cents
  - [U4] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py:109, in reconcile_monthly_totals: compares it with _bought_this_month(account), where _bought_this_month(account) returns sum(purchase.price_cents for purchase in account.purchases if purchase.in_current_month)
  - [U5] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/spend_reconciliation.py:115, in _the_disagreement_in: subtracts with it: _bought_this_month(account) - account.total_this_month_cents, where _bought_this_month(account) returns sum(purchase.price_cents for purchase in account.purchases if purchase.in_current_month)
  - [U6] total_this_month_cents at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, in average_spend_per_item_this_month: divides with it: account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)
  - Where [F1] says otherwise of these lines, they stand.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
  - AI-2 (mitigate, open): Put monthly-spend-feature back
Rewriting what the incident wrote wrong is left to a person by design: say it in still_at_risk and the action items, never under went_wrong.
PR #355 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P1] - suspected, not confirmed.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

system.text:
You write the postmortem for an incident Argus has already handled. One message describes it - what Argus did and read, the candidate causes, the actions and what they came to, and every figure already measured - and you answer by calling submit_postmortem. Nothing is left to look up.

The candidates are the Investigator's account, written while the incident ran and before anything was tried. The record - the lines saying what Argus did, the changes, the log lines, the actions and their verdicts - is what happened. Where the two disagree, the record is right.

Write causal_chain as the five whys. The first step is the symptom: what the people using the service saw, with the evidence that shows it. The symptom field is that step in a few words, and the two must agree. Each step after it answers why the step before happened - one cause, no jumps - and cites its evidence from the record, never a candidate: a candidate is a hypothesis, and the chain says what happened. Five is a guide, not a quota: stop where the evidence stops. The root_cause field says the mechanism: the step of the chain that says why the change broke the service.

A why the record cannot answer - a missing test, a missing safeguard, an alert that came late - is a contributing factor rather than a step, and each contributing factor names an action item that answers it. Where one why has several answers, follow the one that leads to the fault and make the others contributing factors.

Never stop at a person. Where somebody's action set the incident off, ask why the system let that action do harm - why it was possible at all - and carry on from there.

tools.description: Submit the postmortem for this incident. Every field is required. Write no figure yourself anywhere in your answer - no time, duration, percentage, count or amount, not in digits and not spelled out in words. Every figure you are shown is followed by its name in braces, like {A3} or {duration}: where your prose states one, write its name, braces and all, and the document writes the figure in. A figure you were not shown but could work out from two you were - the span between two instants, how far one share is above another, how many times one is the other - is written as that working, braces and all: {back_to_normal - began}, {T3.1 - alert_raised}, {errors_at_worst / errors_before}. The document works it out from the figures as you were shown them. Say any other size with no number in it, not even in a word - "most requests", "for several minutes", never "twenty minutes", "a third" or "tripled". A number is a figure even with a unit or a clock's marks on it (5m, 10ms, 3x, 12:05Z). Any other word with a digit in it is a name - a label you cite (T2, G3fa2, C1, AI-1), a version (v2), a revision, a pod - and is written as given. State only what the evidence you are shown says: where the record does not show something - a check that was or was not run, how many replicas - leave it out or say it was not seen.

action_items.description: What should be done that the record does not already hold, each one thing a person could take on: two things to do are two items. Empty where the record's own items answer every factor. Propose nothing to confirm a cause the record already confirmed - a mitigation that worked, a hypothesis marked confirmed - and no check of what the evidence you are shown already shows: a diff states what changed. Where an F row says to check something a D row shows, say what the D row shows, and the item is what follows from it.

answers.description: The labels of the contributing factors it answers: CF-1. Empty where it answers none.

assumptions.description: Anything else the reader should know was assumed rather than measured. Empty is a valid answer.

causal_chain.description: The cause as the five whys, from the symptom down: the first step is what users saw - or, where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, that and what was seen instead - and each step after it answers why the step directly before it happened. The first why says why the symptom happened, not the symptom again in more detail. Where the incident needed two things at once - something going wrong, and nothing in place to contain it - follow the one that leads to what set it off; the other is one of the contributing_factors, not named in the chain. A safeguard that did not stop it is never a step of its own: it is one of the contributing_factors. Every step cites at least one piece of evidence by its label. Date a change by its own row's instant - the T or P row that records it - never by an effect it had. A state a row read - how many replicas run a revision, which way a flag is set - is known as of the row that read it, by that row's instant, which is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's - not from when the change was made. What else the record ruled out - an earlier change, a flag the provider showed unchanged, a candidate refuted - goes in the ruled_out of the step that ties the incident to the change that set it off, citing what ruled it out, and never as a step. An earlier change is ruled out only by the service measured healthy with it in place - in metrics read between it and the onset, in an alert that dates the first harm itself at or after a later change (at, where the two instants are the same), or after a confirmed action that left it there - never by how long before the onset it came. Where the record shows none of these, it was not ruled out: say so in that step itself. Stop where the evidence stops.

cites.description: The labels of the evidence that shows this step: T3, G3fa2. Not rows that merely happened at the same time.

ruled_out.description: What else the record ruled out at this step, each what it was and why. Empty on every step but the one that ties the incident to the change that set it off.

cites.description: The labels of what ruled it out.

cause_in_plain_words.description: What caused the incident, in one sentence for a reader who does not work on the service: no component names unless they are unavoidable. When it began, for how long, how bad it got, what customers lost and what was done the document says itself - say none of them. Say only what the record says - of a change, of the service, of the people - and nothing it does not. Where part of it rests only on a reading nothing ran, say that part as likely, in plain words, without mentioning the reading.

cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading.description: Whether the mechanism in root_cause rests on an F row - a reading of the code nothing ran - with no S or D row showing what it rests on. Where you answer true, the document says itself, beside the root cause, that the cause is unverified, and leaves its root-cause review box for a person: say neither in root_cause.

contributing_factors.description: Conditions that had to hold for the incident to happen and did not cause it alone - a safeguard that did not stop it, a gap in detection or review. A factor held before the incident began: what the response did, declined or left behind - an action taken or not, automatic sync left off - is not one; where it went wrong, say it under went_wrong. Not the root cause again in other words: a factor is something that, had it been otherwise, would have stopped or shortened the incident even with what root_cause says still true. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. An alert finds what its rule watches, not the cause behind it: say a fault was found only by what the record shows found it. Each is answered by at least one action item: one of the record's, named in its addressed_by, or one you propose, whose answers name it.

addressed_by.description: The record's own action items that answer it, by the numbers the record gives them: AI-1. Empty where none of them does. Never an item you propose: that item names, in its own answers, the factors it answers.

had_it_been_otherwise.description: What would have gone differently had this been otherwise - stopped, shortened or caught sooner - with what root_cause says still true. A factor that only says the root cause again cannot answer this: leave it out of the list.

label.description: CF-1 for the first factor, CF-2 for the next, and so on in the order you give them. Written here and in an item's answers, never in your prose: the reader never sees it.

lessons.description: What went well, what went wrong, and where the incident got lucky - a risk that went unnoticed this time. Any list may be empty. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. How soon the alert came is weighed by the document already, from what was measured: say nothing of it here.

got_lucky.description: Something the record shows went the fortunate way by chance, and would have made it worse had it not. Empty where the record shows none. Not what kind of fault it was, which the impact already says, nor a limit of what the record shows, which is said in assumptions as what was assumed. Not how the service did over a stretch its metrics did not cover, nor what a failure there would have done - the document says how it did.

went_well.description: Where one says how quickly Argus did something, write the span as a working of two instants - a T or P row's instant is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's: {T3.1 - alert_raised}, not in words ("within seconds"). Set the span beside what it times - the thing its later instant dates - not after something else in the same sentence: "Argus confirmed, {T20.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, that the rollback had brought the service back", not "Argus confirmed the rollback had brought the service back from the incident's level {T20.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised". Name what Code-Fix proposed without saying what it does: the action items and Code-Fix's own reading say that, with its conditions.

went_wrong.description: A change the response left in place on purpose, which one of the record's own action items undoes (automatic sync left off), went as designed and did not go wrong; so did what the design leaves to a person - a draft fix to review and merge. Not a limit of what the record shows - logs nobody read, metrics that stop short of the onset: the document says what was read, and anything assumed is said in assumptions. Not the root cause or a contributing factor again - the document says those already.

reaches_a_cause.description: Whether the chain says why the change that set the incident off broke the service, rather than stopping at that change. A step resting on F rows - a reading of the code nothing ran - counts: whether that leaves the cause unverified is cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading's to say. That a new version does worse is what the change did, not why it broke the service: answer false where the chain says the evidence does not show why.

root_cause.description: What caused the incident, in one or two sentences, written for an engineer who was not on the call: the mechanism - why the change that set it off broke the service, as far as the evidence goes, a missing protection or not. Not the trigger, how it was confirmed, what resolved it or what was ruled out - the document states each of those itself. Not one of the contributing_factors: a safeguard that would have stopped it with this mechanism unchanged is said there, not here. What the service did over the stretch the metrics did not watch is not the mechanism: the document says it itself. Whether it was verified the document says itself, from your answer to cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading - do not say it.

still_at_risk.description: What was still at risk at the end of the time Argus held the incident, in one sentence for the same reader - what the fault still in place then could yet do, or the same thing able to happen again. Empty where nothing was. Not whether the service or its metrics were back, nor why - the summary says both. Not what Argus left to a person - a draft fix, automatic sync left off, a recommended action - which the document says itself. Say only what the record says: nothing of the service after that was read.

symptom.description: What went wrong as somebody using the service saw it, as short as it can be: it is the document's title. One sentence with no number in it, never over 16 words - the thing that went wrong and what happened to it, with an active verb: 'Account pages failed'. Not the metric the alert fired on, not the cause - the document adds the change it began with itself, after your sentence and a 'while', so end on what went wrong, with no clause after it - and not how it was found, which the document's Detection says. Where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, say that and what was seen instead, in that one sentence.

tools.name: submit_postmortem
